The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, along with a new record for the U.S. with more than 1,000 private unicorn companies.

A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S.
Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.
Leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one new unicorn.
The most valuable of the newly minted unicorns were electrical infrastructure company Axiom Solutions International , TypeSafe AI a model developer of Jev, and agentic AI assistant company Manus AI .
Familiar names topped the list of investors backing the latest cohort. Andreessen Horowitz has led rounds across seven portfolio companies over time, Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst in four companies and Eclipse three companies from this batch.
New unicorns in October 2026
Here are October’s new unicorn companies by industry segment.
AI models, assistants and agents
TypeSafe AI : San Francisco-based AI model developer TypeSafe AI raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with participation from DCVC and Sequoia Capital. The 2-year-old company develops an AI model Jev for structured decision-making, helping applications automate tasks such as classification, scoring and routing with confidence estimates.
Manus AI : Singapore-based AI assistant Manus AI raised $500 million at a $4 billion valuation. Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the round. The 3-year-old company develops general-purpose AI agents that perform tasks including research, browser automation, content creation and software development. Meta agreed to acquire Manus in December 2025, but Chinese regulators intervened and ordered the transaction reversed.
Nous Research : Austin-based Nous Research, developer of the Hermes agent, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the financing, with investors including Nvidia , Microsoft’s M12 , Menlo Ventures and Union Square Ventures . The 3-year-old company develops open-source AI models, agents and infrastructure for AI development and deployment. Nous Research built the open-source Hermes Agent, which it is deploying for businesses.
Upstage : South Korea-based Upstage, developer of the open-source Solar model, raised $30 million in Series C funding, reaching $1.5 billion in value. The 6-year-old company develops the Solar language models and document-processing technology that converts unstructured business information into usable data for the future of work.
Wabi : San Francisco-based personal AI assistant Wabi raised a $55 million Series A at a $1.25 billion valuation. IVP led the financing, joined by investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Forerunner and Amazon’s Alexa Fund . The 1-year-old company develops an AI personal assistant for everyday activities such as planning trips, coordinating meals and organizing tasks.
Town : San Francisco-based Town, a developer of a workforce AI assistant, raised a $108 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation. Forerunner and Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, First Round Capital and other investors. The 2-year-old company develops personalized AI assistants that connect with workplace tools across teams to manage email, prepare meeting briefings, organize schedules and complete recurring tasks.
Aerospace, defense and space
Air Space Intelligence : Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which makes AI software for national security, raised a $325 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation. Spark Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Citadel Securities , Craft Ventures , Energy Impact Partners and Meritech Capital Partners . The 8-year-old company develops AI software for managing complex physical operations across aviation, defense, energy and logistics.
Xona : Burlingame, California-based Xona, which says it’s developing a better satellite navigation system, raised a $250 million Series D at a $2.45 billion valuation. Future Ventures led the round, with participation from Industrious Ventures and Woven Capital . The 7-year-old company says it’s developing a low Earth orbit satellite network to deliver precise positioning, navigation and timing services for applications including defense, transportation and autonomous systems.
Firehawk Aerospace : Dallas-based munitions manufacturer Firehawk Aerospace raised a $150 million Series D at a $1.4 billion valuation. Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.
On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.
Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut.
An IPO and a private placement
The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans.
For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.
Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC .
Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
Revenue and recent updates
Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.
For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.
The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.
As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

HAMBURG, Germany , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- H.I.G. Capital ("H.I.G."), a leading global private capital firm with $76 billion of capital under management, is pleased to announce that an affiliate has signed a definitive agreement to acquire a majority stake in go asia ("go asia" or the "Company"), Germany's largest retail chain for Asian food. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The transaction is subject to customary regulatory approvals.
Founded in 2008 and headquartered in Berlin, go asia operates over 70 stores in more than 30 cities across Germany. With a range of over 10,000 products from across Asia and more than 1,600 employees, the Company addresses the growing demand for authentic Asian cuisine from a well-diversified customer base.
H.I.G. and the founding family led by Wengui Ye have agreed to enter into a partnership to accelerate the Company's next phase of growth. H.I.G. will contribute its retail and consumer expertise, international network, and capital resources to support go asia's dynamic store network expansion in Germany and Europe. The founding family will reinvest and retain a significant ownership interest in the Company, and founder Wengui Ye and the Company's management team will continue to play an active role in shaping go asia's future.
Wengui Ye, founder of go asia, commented: "When I opened our first store in Berlin in 2009, my vision was to bring authentic Asian cuisine to German homes. Today, I am proud that go asia is Germany's largest Asian food retailer – and we still see significant untapped growth potential both in Germany and especially across Europe. With its vast retail experience, strong international network, and partnership-oriented, operational approach, H.I.G. is the ideal partner for our next stage of growth. My family and I will remain significantly invested, and I look forward to continuing to shape the future of go asia together with H.I.G. and our outstanding team."
Christian Kraul-von Renner, Managing Director at H.I.G., remarked: "go asia is an impressive founder-led success story. Wengui Ye and his team have built Germany's largest Asian food retailer with an authentic product range and a distinctive, scalable store concept. We see significant potential to expand the store network in Germany as well as to enter other European markets. Together with the Ye family and the management team, we look forward to accelerating go asia's next phase of growth."
About go asia
Founded by Wengui Ye in Berlin in 2008, go asia opened its first store in Berlin-Charlottenburg in 2009. Today, with over 70 stores in more than 30 cities and over 1,600 employees, go asia is Germany's largest retail chain for Asian food. Its stores are located predominantly in city-center locations, shopping centers, and transport hubs, complemented by an online shop. The Company's assortment comprises over 10,000 products from across Asia, ranging from rice, noodles, sauces, and spices to frozen and fresh products, beverages, and kitchenware. For more information, please visit the go asia website at goasia.net .

H.I.G.'s debt funds invest in senior, unitranche, and junior debt financing to companies across the size spectrum, both on a primary (direct origination) basis, as well as in the secondary markets.
H.I.G.'s real estate funds invest in value-added properties, which can benefit from improved asset management practices.
H.I.G. Infrastructure focuses on making value-add and core plus investments in the infrastructure sector.
Since its founding in 1993, H.I.G. has invested in and managed more than 400 companies worldwide. The Firm's current portfolio includes more than 100 companies with combined sales in excess of $53 billion. For more information, please refer to the H.I.G. website at hig.com .

candidates.title: Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
candidates.snippet: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.

Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
Gené Teare
November 9, 2026
Gené Teare
@geneteare

More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.
The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.
Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)
That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.
The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.
At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.
“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan , a partner at Scale Venture Partners , which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.
This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.
Go big and early — or wait
Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.
With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.
Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”
Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.
The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.
“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”
Deals sizes trend higher
At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.
Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.
Raising a large Series A
For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.
“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures , whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.
“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.
She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.
But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

Mercor Hits $20B Valuation After $750M Series D to Train and Test AI Agents
By James Dargan · 11 November 2026 · 1 min read
AI training startup Mercor has secured $750 million in a Series D funding round that values the company at $20 billion, the firm said on Tuesday. Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, Nvidia and funds managed by affiliates of Apollo were among the participants.
The San Francisco-based company started out as an AI-powered hiring platform but now connects technology companies with subject-matter experts whose knowledge is used to train, test and improve AI models and agents. Mercor said the new capital will go towards training and testing AI agents on professional tasks.
Co-CEO Brendan Foody said every job in the economy will require its own AI agents, and every company will need a way to train and evaluate those agents on its own work.
The latest valuation roughly doubles the approximately $10 billion figure Mercor reached after raising $350 million in October last year. The company counts Jack Dorsey and venture capitalist Peter Thiel among its backers.
The deal reflects strong investor appetite for AI, which has driven a sharp rise in private funding this year and produced a growing group of heavily capitalised startups with multibillion-dollar valuations. According to Crunchbase, AI-driven startups raised $102 billion in the third quarter of 2026, accounting for 64% of global venture capital.

By Sam Tabahriti
LONDON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – AI chip startup Fractile was valued at $7 billion in its latest fundraising round, which included backing from the British government, a person involved ​in the deal said on Wednesday, making it one ‌of Britain’s most valuable technology startups.
The London- and Bristol-based company is developing chips designed to improve AI inference, the process through which AI models generate responses. Fractile says its technology can deliver faster performance while cutting energy use ‌and ​costs.
The company raised $720 million in a Series ⁠C funding round led ⁠by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, it told Reuters.
Other investors included Google’s venture arm CapitalG, BlackRock, DST Global, Elad Gil, Balderton, SV Angel, Britain’s Sovereign AI fund and the ​British Business Bank.
BRITAIN’S AI AMBITIONS
The investment marks a major vote of confidence in Britain’s efforts to build domestic AI infrastructure, rather ⁠than solely relying on overseas suppliers ⁠for the computing power that underpins the technology.
It also ​highlights growing investor interest in companies developing the hardware behind AI, ​a market dominated by Nvidia and a handful of Asian ‌semiconductor manufacturers.
Britain has made becoming an AI superpower a key part of its economic strategy, seeking to build on strengths in AI research and chip design while retaining more of the jobs, ⁠investment and economic value generated by the technology.
“For too long, Britain has produced some of the world’s best scientific ideas, only to see too ⁠much of the ‌technology, industry and wealth they create built elsewhere,” ⁠AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said in a statement ​on the ‌funding round.
“We are determined to change that.”
Britain is ​home to ⁠chip designer Arm, whose technology is used in billions of devices worldwide, but its semiconductor manufacturing industry remains small compared with those in the US and Asia.
Fractile plans to launch its first commercial chip next year.

Private equity firm EQT-backed Indian renewable energy platform Resolven on Tuesday said it has mobilised USD 900 million (about Rs 8,550 crore) financing this year so far, backed by an expanding lender base.
The funds have been mobilized from a set of 15 lenders including public sector banks, private banks, MNC banks and infrastructure financing institutions, a company statement said.

Of USD 900 million, about USD 700 million is fund-based debt financing, and USD 200 million group level non-fund lines.

We are grateful for the trust placed by lenders on us and gives us the strength to deliver on what we have promised."
Resolven is targeting more than 1.5 GW of new renewable capacity annually across solar, wind, hybrid and battery storage, and aims to reach 10 GW by 2030.
It is powered by EQT, one of the world’s largest private markets firms, with 270 billion euros in total assets under management. Comments

candidates.title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
candidates.snippet: Fractile has now become one of the top-funded players in the race for purpose-built AI chips.
candidates.text:
Fractile , a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated .
Alongside the likes of Axelera , Etched , and OLIX , this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.
However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.
As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source .
Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot , its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual tradeoff between memory and capacity.
This tradeoff has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.
In a LinkedIn post , Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

candidates.text:
Peloton: $700 Million Senior Secured Notes Offering Upsized From $600 Million As Part Of Debt Refinancing
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 8:20 AM
Peloton: $700 Million Senior Secured Notes Offering Upsized From $600 Million As Part Of Debt Refinancing
Peloton Interactive has announced the pricing of an upsized $700 million senior secured notes offering carrying an annual interest rate of 8.625% and maturing in 2032. The offering, increased from an originally announced $600 million, is part of a broader refinancing initiative that also includes a proposed $200 million revolving credit facility.
The New York-based connected fitness company expects the notes offering to generate approximately $700 million in gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions, and other transaction expenses.
The transaction is expected to settle on November 20, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions.
Peloton intends to use the net proceeds, together with existing cash, to repay all outstanding borrowings under its current $1 billion five-year term loan facility.
The existing term loan agreement will be terminated following repayment.
The refinancing is designed to restructure Peloton’s debt obligations by replacing its outstanding term loans with senior secured notes carrying a maturity date in 2032.
The notes will represent senior secured obligations of the company, meaning they will benefit from specified collateral arrangements and rank according to the terms established in the financing documents.
The annual interest rate of 8.625% determines the stated interest expense associated with the notes.
At the full $700 million principal amount, the stated annual interest obligation would total approximately $60.4 million before considering any applicable adjustments or other financing costs.
The refinancing also includes Peloton’s proposed entry into a new $200 million revolving credit facility with a five-year term.
A revolving credit facility allows a company to borrow, repay, and potentially borrow again within an established credit limit, subject to the agreement’s terms.
Such facilities can provide financial flexibility for working capital needs, operating expenses, and other corporate requirements.
Peloton’s proposed revolving facility would complement its longer-term debt financing by providing an additional source of potential liquidity.
However, the company emphasized that completion of the senior secured notes offering is not dependent on entering into the new revolving credit facility.
The notes offering is also not conditioned on repayment of the existing term loan facility.
These provisions allow the offering to close independently of the other components of the broader refinancing initiative.
Expanded Offering And Use Of Proceeds
Peloton increased the offering from $600 million to $700 million, representing an additional $100 million in planned debt issuance.
The expansion provides additional proceeds that can be applied toward the company’s refinancing requirements.
Peloton plans to combine the proceeds with cash on hand to repay the remaining loans outstanding under its existing term loan facility and cover associated transaction expenses.
The announced $1 billion figure refers to the size of the existing facility rather than a confirmed amount currently outstanding.
Consequently, the company has not specified the precise cash contribution required to complete the repayment.
Following the refinancing, any remaining net proceeds may be used for general corporate purposes.
Potential uses include working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions, and other business opportunities.
Peloton also identified possible repurchases of its Class A common stock among the permitted uses of remaining proceeds.
These potential applications provide flexibility for management to allocate capital according to future corporate priorities.
The company’s financing plan reflects an effort to manage its capital structure while preserving resources for ongoing operations and strategic initiatives.
By extending a portion of its debt obligations through 2032, Peloton is seeking to establish a longer-term financing structure.
The company has not announced specific acquisitions, capital expenditure projects, or share repurchases associated with any remaining proceeds.
Private Placement Structure
The senior secured notes are being offered through a private placement rather than a registered public securities offering.
Eligible purchasers include qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A of the Securities Act of 1933.
The offering is also available to certain investors outside the United States pursuant to Regulation S.
These provisions establish the regulatory framework for distributing the notes to eligible institutional and international investors.
The financing remains subject to customary closing conditions.
Peloton’s expanded $700 million debt offering and proposed $200 million revolving credit facility represent significant components of its broader refinancing strategy.
The transactions are intended to replace existing term loan obligations, extend the company’s debt maturity profile, and provide additional financial flexibility as it manages its capital structure and future business requirements.

candidates.text:
OneWater Marine: $547 Million Inventory Financing Facility And Term Loan Extended Through 2029
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 8:19 AM
OneWater Marine: $547 Million Inventory Financing Facility And Term Loan Extended Through 2029
OneWater Marine, one of the largest premium marine retailers in the United States, has amended its senior secured term loan and floor plan credit facilities to extend their maturities by two years while increasing its inventory financing capacity by $50 million. The amendments raise the company’s available floor plan financing capacity to as much as $547 million, providing additional financial flexibility as OneWater focuses on inventory management and balance-sheet improvements.
Under the amended agreements, the maturity of OneWater’s senior secured term loan has been extended to July 31, 2029, while its floor plan credit facility will now mature on March 1, 2029.
The extensions provide additional time before the company must address the scheduled maturities of these financing arrangements.
Truist Bank continues to lead the senior secured term loan facility, while Wells Fargo remains the lead lender for the floor plan financing arrangement. The expansion of inventory financing capacity also includes the addition of a new lender to the lending syndicate.
Both facilities remain subject to customary financial and non-financial covenants.
Expanded Inventory Financing Capacity
The increase in floor plan financing capacity is particularly relevant to OneWater’s retail operations, which depend on maintaining inventories of new and pre-owned boats across its dealership network.
Floor plan financing is a specialized form of credit commonly used by vehicle and marine retailers to finance inventory before products are sold to customers.
Rather than using operating cash to purchase every boat held in inventory, retailers can use these financing arrangements to support the acquisition and management of available products.
As inventory is sold, the associated financing obligations are generally repaid according to the terms of the lending agreements.
This structure allows retailers to maintain product availability while managing working capital requirements.
OneWater’s amended agreement increases its maximum inventory financing capacity from approximately $497 million to $547 million.
The additional $50 million provides potential borrowing capacity to support inventory requirements across the company’s operations.
However, the expanded facility represents available financing capacity rather than an immediate increase in cash or an indication that the entire amount has been borrowed.
The company believes the additional flexibility will help it manage inventory levels more effectively as it navigates challenging conditions in the marine retail market.
Focus On Balance-Sheet Strengthening
The amendments reflect OneWater’s efforts to improve its financial flexibility and extend its debt maturity profile.
By pushing the maturities of both facilities into 2029, the company has reduced near-term refinancing pressures associated with these arrangements.
Management indicated that the changes are part of a broader strategy to strengthen the balance sheet and maintain appropriate inventory levels.
Inventory management is an important consideration for marine retailers because boats represent relatively expensive products that can require substantial financing.
Demand can also be influenced by consumer confidence, interest rates, financing availability, and broader economic conditions.
Maintaining an appropriate balance between available inventory and expected customer demand can help retailers manage borrowing requirements and operating expenses.
OneWater expects the amended facilities to provide greater flexibility as it enters fiscal 2027.
The company intends to remain focused on maintaining suitable inventory levels while continuing efforts to strengthen its financial position.
OneWater’s Nationwide Retail Operations
Headquartered in Buford, Georgia, OneWater Marine operates 88 retail locations and six distribution centers and warehouses across 17 states.
The company also maintains multiple online marketplaces supporting its retail activities.
Its geographic footprint includes several states ranked among the nation’s largest markets for marine retail expenditures.
OneWater sells new and pre-owned boats while providing a range of related products and services.
Its revenue sources include boat sales, financing and insurance products, parts and accessories, maintenance, repairs, and other marine services.
This diversified operating model allows the company to generate revenue from both boat purchases and ongoing customer relationships.
The amended lending arrangements support the financing infrastructure underlying these operations.
With its term loan maturity extended to July 2029, floor plan maturity extended to March 2029, and inventory financing capacity increased to $547 million, OneWater has secured additional time and flexibility to manage its capital structure.
The company plans to use that flexibility to support disciplined inventory management while addressing the challenges affecting the marine retail industry.
KEY QUOTE:
“Extending maturities for both facilities and expanding our floor plan capacity reflect our progress in strengthening our balance sheet and the continued support of our lending partners. The amendments give us added flexibility to effectively manage our inventory as we navigate this challenging retail environment. As we move into fiscal 2027, we remain focused on maintaining proper inventory levels and fortifying the balance sheet.”
Jack Ezzell, Chief Operating Officer And Chief Financial Officer Of OneWater Marine

LPL Financial Brings In $390 Million Firm Contour Wealth Management
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 4:36 PM
LPL Financial Brings In $390 Million Firm Contour Wealth Management
LPL Financial has added Contour Wealth Management, a Pennsylvania-based financial advisory practice serving approximately $390 million in client assets, to its broker-dealer and registered investment advisory platforms. Financial advisor Joe Borgese, a certified financial planner, joins LPL from Cetera alongside a team focused on comprehensive financial planning and multigenerational client relationships.
Contour Wealth Management is based in Boyertown, Pennsylvania, outside Philadelphia.
The firm serves individuals and families, including educators, healthcare professionals, business owners, and clients across multiple generations.
Its planning approach emphasizes developing long-term relationships and adapting financial strategies as clients’ needs evolve.
Borgese began his career in financial services in 1990, initially working in banking before moving into other areas of the industry.
Over more than three decades, he has developed a practice centered on investment planning, retirement strategies, and broader financial guidance.
Contour Wealth Management works with some families across three generations, helping clients address financial needs ranging from retirement planning to college savings.
The practice begins each client engagement by establishing an understanding of the client’s goals, expectations, and personal circumstances.
Advisors then develop financial plans intended to adapt to changes involving careers, families, retirement, and other life events.
The firm’s services include financial planning, investment planning, and tax preparation, supported by working relationships with outside professionals.
The practice is supported by an experienced team that coordinates client relationships and ongoing financial planning needs.
Lindsey Borgese, also a certified financial planner, helps manage the office.
The team includes Diana C. Dugan, an enrolled agent, alongside Brian Christman, Cheryl Dietz, and Karen Walla.
Their responsibilities support client service, administration, and coordination across the firm’s financial planning activities.
Reasons For Joining LPL Financial
Contour Wealth Management selected LPL Financial based on its technology infrastructure, operational support, and advisor-focused service model.
The practice also identified potential cost efficiencies for clients as an important consideration.
LPL provides brokerage, advisory, technology, and practice management services to independent financial advisors and financial institutions.
Its infrastructure is designed to allow advisors to operate their businesses while accessing a broader range of investment products and operational resources.
For Contour Wealth Management, the transition provides access to additional technology and support capabilities while preserving its relationship-driven planning approach.
Borgese believes these resources will help the practice operate more efficiently and continue delivering personalized financial guidance.
The move also reflects the broader appeal of independent advisory platforms that allow practices to maintain their identity while benefiting from the resources of larger financial services organizations.
Financial advisors increasingly evaluate technology, compliance assistance, service capabilities, and operating costs when selecting affiliation partners.
LPL has been expanding its platform through the recruitment of independent advisors and advisory teams.
The company supports more than 32,000 financial advisors and the wealth management practices of approximately 1,100 financial institutions.
Its platform services and custodies approximately $2.6 trillion in brokerage and advisory assets on behalf of approximately eight million Americans.
LPL offers multiple advisor affiliation models, allowing practices to select structures aligned with their business needs.
Contour Wealth Management’s addition increases LPL’s presence in Pennsylvania while bringing an established practice with approximately $390 million in client assets.
The relationship will allow Borgese and his team to continue serving clients while using LPL’s technology, operating infrastructure, and advisor support resources.
KEY QUOTES:
“Our clients’ lives don’t move in a straight line, and their financial plans shouldn’t be static either. We start by understanding what they want their life to look like, then build a plan around those goals and continue adapting it as life changes. Our team has known many of these families for years, and in some cases across generations. That familiarity allows us to be there for the next decision, the next transition and the next step in their journey.”
Joe Borgese, Financial Advisor At Contour Wealth Management
“The biggest consideration for me was what this move could mean for our clients. LPL’s combination of technology, operational support and the team-based approach to supporting advisors gives us an opportunity to work more efficiently. Just as important, we believe this move can help us deliver value to clients while allowing our team to stay focused on the relationships we’ve built.”
Joe Borgese, Financial Advisor At Contour Wealth Management
“Contour Wealth Management, LLC has built a deeply personal practice around continuity, comprehensive planning and relationships that extend across generations. Joe and his team understand that every family’s path is different, and they have created an experience designed to evolve alongside clients through each stage of life. We’re pleased to welcome Contour Wealth Management, LLC to LPL and look forward to supporting the team with the technology, resources and operational scale to preserve those trusted relationships while building for the future.”
Marc Cohen, Chief Growth Officer At LPL Financial

UA Little Rock: $266.5 Million Centennial Campaign Exceeds Fundraising Goal
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 1:31 AM
UA Little Rock: $266.5 Million Centennial Campaign Exceeds Fundraising Goal
The University of Arkansas at Little Rock has completed its Centennial Campaign with $266.5 million raised, surpassing its $250 million goal and setting a fundraising record for the university.
The seven-year campaign attracted 22,762 donors who made 197,887 contributions. University leaders announced the final total of $266,532,569.07 during a November 5 celebration recognizing donors, alumni and community partners.
The campaign established 211 endowments and helped increase the university’s endowment by 192%. Its investments span scholarships, student support, academic leadership, research and campus facilities.
Private support helped launch the Half-Off Scholarship, which reduced tuition costs for incoming freshmen, and the Trojan Guarantee, which covers remaining tuition for qualifying students receiving both a Pell Grant and the Arkansas Academic Challenge Scholarship.
A $7.5 million Windgate Foundation gift established the Enduring Opportunity Scholarship Program to help sustain the university’s affordability initiatives.
Academic investments included endowed directorships supporting nursing, education and engineering. The university also expanded simulation-based nursing education and developed a year-long paid teacher residency program.
Campus improvements included the revitalization of Trojan Way and renovations to 22 classrooms and laboratories. The Shellam Flake planetarium is scheduled for a soft opening in December 2026.
The fundraising effort included more than 19,000 face-to-face visits by the development team with donors and prospective supporters. Campaign co-chairs Alfred Williams and Jerry Damerow helped lead the initiative alongside university leadership and a broader campaign cabinet.
The new endowments will provide continuing support after the campaign’s conclusion, extending its effects beyond immediate construction projects and scholarship awards to future students, faculty and academic programs.
KEY QUOTES:
“Seven years ago, a $250 million campaign for UA Little Rock might have seemed out of reach. Tonight, we celebrate not just reaching that goal, but what reaching it says about who we have become.”
Christina S. Drale, Chancellor Of The University Of Arkansas At Little Rock
“Those investments have changed UA Little Rock forever. They have helped us become stronger, more innovative and better positioned to serve our students than ever before.”
Christina S. Drale, Chancellor Of The University Of Arkansas At Little Rock

candidates.text:
DeepTech
Swiss VC Redalpine Raises $250 Million for A.I., Robotics and Biotech
Jakob Steinschaden , co-produced by AI 10. November 2026, 08:00
The redalpine team, which has closed its eighth early-stage fund at $250 million. © redalpine

While many venture capital firms spend months courting investors, Redalpine was done in less than a year: The Swiss firm has closed its eighth early-stage fund, Redalpine Capital VIII (RAC VIII), at $250 million. The fund was oversubscribed and is larger than its predecessor, which closed at $200 million in 2024. Redalpine now manages more than $1.4 billion in total.
Where the Money Is Going
With RAC VIII, Redalpine plans to invest in about 20 European start-ups at the seed to Series A stage, selected from more than 5,000 companies it reviews each year. Checks range from $1 million to $15 million, and Redalpine often leads the rounds. The focus is on companies at the intersection of software and science. Half of the investment team has a background in the natural sciences or engineering, according to Redalpine.
The first three investments from the new fund:
Enact Intelligence: The Zurich robotics start-up aims to give robots a sense of touch and recently raised a $30 million pre-seed round with backing from Yann LeCun, among others.
Helical: The London start-up is building a virtual A.I. lab for drug discovery. Redalpine previously led its $10 million seed round .
Arlequin AI: The team, based in Paris, Berlin and London, is developing an A.I. architecture to protect critical systems and works with government agencies.
Sebastian Becker, a general partner, said artificial intelligence was leveling the playing field for founders around the world, giving the edge to those who best understand the science behind a product and the hardest problems.
Aviva, Flexstone and KfW as Backers
The limited partners in RAC VIII include existing and new investors, among them the British asset manager Aviva Investors, Flexstone Partners and the German development bank KfW. Redalpine was founded in Zurich in 2006, is now based in Zug and has offices in Berlin and London.
Its portfolio includes well-known names such as Mistral AI, N26 and Proxima Fusion. Redalpine led the Munich fusion start-up’s seed round, and in the summer, Proxima raised €411 million at a €2.4 billion valuation . Since 2023, Redalpine says it has sold or taken public 12 portfolio companies. They include the Swiss biotech Araris, which the Japanese drugmaker Taiho acquired for up to $1.14 billion , and, according to Redalpine, Memo Therapeutics (to Ipsen) and the A.I. security start-up Lakera (to Check Point). Companies from its previous fund, RAC VII, have raised more than $1.1 billion from investors in total.
The Competition
Redalpine is not the only firm raising fresh capital for European tech start-ups this year. In Zurich, Lakestar closed Lakestar Resilience I, a $300 million fund for defense and dual-use technologies. Headline raised $400 million for its eighth fund, which targets seed and Series A rounds in A.I., and Accel’s new European fund comes to $800 million. In Germany, Uplift Ventures launched a €100 million deep-tech fund that also invests in seed to Series A rounds.
Money Flows to Established Players
Fund-raising remains difficult for many venture firms, however. European venture funds raised $14.9 billion across 111 funds through the end of September 2026, compared with $15.5 billion in all of last year, according to PitchBook data compiled by SeedBlink . The money is concentrating in the largest funds, and the market beyond them remains tight, according to PitchBook. In the DACH region, 83 venture funds closed with a combined €6.2 billion in 2022, while in the first nine months of 2025, only 21 funds closed with €2.0 billion, according to PitchBook. The median time from launch to final close is 26 months.
That favors established firms with a record of exits, such as Redalpine, while new and smaller fund managers face a tougher climb. Deep-tech start-ups also often need many years and a lot of capital before they generate revenue or can be sold. Whether the bets on fusion energy, robotics and A.I.-driven biotech pay off will therefore only become clear many years from now.

candidates.snippet: Toronto’s Blue J raises $176-million to expand AI offerings to tax professionals The Globe and Mail
candidates.text:

Rapidly growing Toronto AI software company Blue J Legal Inc. has secured a nine-figure financing for the second straight year as it prepares to offer agentic products to its clientele of tax specialists.
The University of Toronto spinout led by tax law professor Benjamin Alarie has raised a US$176-million financing led by Baltimore-based JMI Equity. U.S. financiers Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures, which co-led a US$122-million investment into Blue J last year, are participating, as well as past backer Intrepid Growth Partners, a Canadian AI-focused investor. The deal, set to be announced Tuesday, values Blue J at US$700-million.
Nearly US$100-million will go to buy shares from employees and early investors. Blue J plans to use its $80-million in proceeds to commercialize its nascent agent product and expand in the U.K. – its third market after the U.S. and Canada – and globally.
Blue J’s main clients are tax accountants, though it also sells to tax lawyers, making it one of several companies bringing AI-driven products to law firms to hasten the automation of often tedious, time-consuming work .
Mr. Alarie, a past associate dean of U of T’s faculty of law, founded Blue J in 2015 with fellow professors Albert Yoon and Anthony Niblett. They worked to develop AI software that would help lawyers and accountants speed up the process of researching complex taxation matters, powered by predictive analytics software. Blue J raised venture capital and generated modest sales.
Then in late 2022 OpenAI launched ChatGPT, the AI chatbot that answered text questions in seconds. Mr. Alarie realized Blue J could fold generative AI capabilities into its product to answer far more tax-research questions. “The technology wasn’t really there to allow us to create a system that could answer any arbitrary tax research question – until we saw the promise of LLMs,” he said.
Blue J rebuilt its product incorporating OpenAI’s large language models, relaunching it in mid-2023. The updated version produced answers in about 90 seconds, but they were wrong about half of the time, a by-product of the quirky tendency of LLMs to generate incorrect information.
The Toronto company set about refining its product, in part by licensing data from Tax Notes, a leading publisher of tax views and commentary, and benefiting from improvements to successive releases of LLMs. Many of its answers come from content licensed by several tax data and information providers, some in exclusive deals.
By the end of 2024, Blue J could produce answers within 10 seconds that were 95-per-cent-plus accurate and its users could have technical back-and-forth conversations about complex tax matters with the program. Some companies found users could save two hours a week each using Blue J, whose individual plans start at US$1,498 a year.
Mr. Alarie said error rates have come down by about 80 per cent this year as measured by “down votes” from users in response to its generated answers, which now occur 0.05 per cent of the time. “We can now confidently deliver an answer to just about any tax research question,” Mr. Alarie said.
Blue J’s increasing speed and accuracy spurred interest, and the number of client firms mushroomed from less than 100 three years ago to more than 1,000 at the end of 2024 and 4,000 a year later. It now serves more than 6,500 firms. Blue J’s annual recurring revenue has expanded by 165 per cent since its last financing in August 2025 and is now in the mid-eight-figure range.
JMI principal Jack Duane said his firm tracked Blue J for years, and received “resounding positive sentiment” when it spoke to its customers, “not just around Blue J’s technology and research platform but also around the company and team. What came through clearly is they are a trusted AI vendor in a space where trust is of the utmost performance.”
Asked of the competitive risk, including the threat that the LLM giants themselves will move into the space, Mr. Duane responded that Blue J’s offering is “extremely hard to replicate” due to its access to proprietary data “and most importantly, their unique domain expertise.”
JMI is one of the most successful foreign investors in the Canadian tech sector. Its portfolio here includes stakes in Clio, Pointclickcare, Jane, Safe Software and Benevity.
Blue J is close to launching its agentic offerings, which will expand its utility beyond simply generating tax answers to clients. Its new workflow product will also enable them to automatically draft other work using its answers, including memos and notices of assessment. “Blue J will be increasingly capable of assisting with just about any of those advisory workflows for which research is an essential input,” Mr. Alarie said.
With reports from Joe Castaldo

candidates.title: Mavria Raises $130M to Date at a $1B Valuation to Build AI Data Centers in a Factory
candidates.snippet: Mavria Raises $130M to Date at a $1B Valuation to Build AI Data Centers in a Factory Wowtale
candidates.text:
Mavria, a startup that wants to build AI data centers in a factory instead of one custom project at a time, has come out of stealth with $130 million raised to date across pre-seed and seed rounds.
Its latest round values the company at $1 billion. Paradigm led it, with participation from AMP PBC, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier and Dream Ventures.
Mavria calls itself “the industrial platform behind American AI.” In an introduction published November 9, co-founder and CEO Adam Blake argued that the AI race is moving from the lab into the physical world. Intelligence needs data centers, data centers need power, and power needs factories, equipment, supply chains and skilled workers, yet much of that infrastructure is still built one custom project at a time on timelines measured in years. America’s labs and clouds have extraordinary ambitions for compute, he wrote, but not the industrial capability to match.
Mavria’s answer is “infrastructure as a product.” It wants to bring engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and capital together so that every project makes it better at delivering the next. Its first product is Terrain, a factory-built data center platform meant to bring compute online faster, with more predictable delivery and lower costs, by replacing custom field construction with repeatable manufacturing. Mavria is building it for frontier labs, cloud providers and data center developers, and says Terrain 01 is in production in Houston now. Press reports describe the platform as 5-megawatt blocks in which power, cooling, controls and IT pods are designed, integrated and tested as one system before shipping, and the Wall Street Journal described it as modular data centers that can be moved by truck.
The founders worked together at the U.S. Department of Energy, where they saw how unprepared American infrastructure is for what is coming. Blake built one of the largest commercial solar companies in the U.S. and sold a software business to Vista Equity Partners. Nick Poradek is an engineer who sold his last company to Liberty Energy and then helped build Liberty’s manufacturing platform. Seth Cohen started as a lawyer at Kirkland and ended up at the center of the effort to restart American nuclear power. The rest of the team has run utilities, led a modular LNG manufacturer with more than a thousand employees, developed major energy projects and scaled technology companies.
“The next decade will show whether America can build at anything close to the pace its AI companies are moving,” Blake wrote. “We’re building Mavria because we don’t want the answer to be no.” The capital will go toward securing critical supply chains, scaling manufacturing and growing the team. Mavria is starting with data centers but says its ambition extends across the physical infrastructure AI depends on, and it is hiring across engineering, manufacturing and operations.
Plenty is still unverified. Mavria did not say how much of the $130 million came in the latest round. Some outlets reported a $100 million round, and a filing with the SEC reportedly shows $75 million sold after a first sale in mid-October. Capacity per unit, pricing, delivery times and customer names have not been disclosed. At least one outlet reported the first facility is not yet running, with testing due in early 2027, which differs from the company’s account. Cohen reportedly said the company was founded in June, which would mean a $1 billion valuation with no disclosed customer deployment.
Racing to industrialize AI infrastructure
Modular AI infrastructure already has several players. Armada, which sells modular data centers for defense and energy customers, raised a $230M Series B in May at a $2 billion valuation. Crusoe raised a $3.9B Series F at a $30.9 billion valuation, and FluidStack raised $1.5B at $18 billion. Singapore’s DayOne and EPG have also reportedly raised large sums for prefabricated data center modules. On the power side, gas-turbine startup Parallax exited stealth with $117 million.
The idea of building in a factory is spreading beyond data centers. Fab2, which wants to mass-produce chip fabs, raised $500M , Valar Atomics raised $1B to bring manufacturing economics to nuclear, and Re:Build raised $2.1B to reindustrialize U.S. manufacturing. Paradigm also co-led drone-delivery company Zipline’s $1.5B round this month, and Sequoia’s recent overhaul points the same way, toward AI and reindustrialization.

Silver Point Capital: $130 Million Financing Supports Riverside’s Hoover CS Acquisition
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 2:17 AM
Silver Point Capital: $130 Million Financing Supports Riverside’s Hoover CS Acquisition
Silver Point Capital’s Direct Lending business has provided a $130 million financing facility supporting The Riverside Company’s acquisition of Hoover Circular Solutions, a provider of packaging, fleet management and logistics services.
Silver Point served as the sole lender for the facility. The financing supports Riverside’s investment in a business serving refining, chemical, energy and industrial customers globally.
Headquartered in Houston, Hoover CS operates a mixed rental fleet of specialized assets across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific. Its services combine packaging equipment with fleet management and logistics support for customers handling industrial materials.
The company’s Catalyst Packaging business provides closed-loop logistics for fresh and spent catalysts used in refineries. Its Chemical Packaging business supplies intermediate bulk containers and intermodal ISO tanks for specialty and hazardous chemicals.
These operations support material handling and transportation requirements across refining and chemical applications. Silver Point cited Hoover CS’s longstanding customer relationships and the role its services play in customers’ operations as factors underlying the financing.
Riverside focuses on businesses at the smaller end of the middle market through private equity and flexible capital strategies. Since its founding in 1988, the firm has completed more than 1,100 investments. Its international portfolios include more than 140 companies.
Founded in 2002, Silver Point oversees more than $52 billion in investable assets across public and private credit strategies and employs more than 400 people.
Its Direct Lending business manages more than $18 billion in investable assets and finances both private equity-backed and sponsorless borrowers. Its mandate covers acquisitions, refinancings and growth capital, among other transactions.
The Hoover CS facility adds to that acquisition financing activity, with Silver Point providing a customized lending solution intended to support operating improvements and growth under Riverside’s ownership.
KEY QUOTE:
“Hoover CS has built a differentiated platform with long-standing customer relationships and solutions serving critical needs for refining and chemical customers. We are pleased to partner with The Riverside Company and provide a customized financing solution to support Hoover CS as it strengthens operations and accelerates growth.”
Anthony DiNello, Head Of Direct Lending At Silver Point Capital

Vaeridion said it had raised €30 million from venture capital investors in its latest funding round. The European Commission had previously made €94.5 million available from its Innovation Fund.
The company is developing a nine-seat passenger aircraft for regional air travel called the Microliner. Vaeridion says it has already received purchase commitments for 130 aircraft.
With the €30 million from investors, Vaeridion wants to build a prototype that is eligible for certification. The EU money is intended for final assembly and for setting up production at the German aviation research and development centre at Oberpfaffenhofen airport. The hub is home to a large branch of the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), and several companies have set up operations nearby.
Vaeridion is aiming to provide a cheaper alternative to the more than 21,000 small, ageing turboprop aircraft that fly on regional routes worldwide. The company's electric aircraft is designed to have a range of 400 kilometres and operate without kerosene.
According to the start-up's calculations, Microliner tickets should cost roughly the same as first-class tickets on Germany's high-speed rail network.
"Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide," said chief executive Ivor von Dartel, a former Airbus manager.
The company says its first customer is the ASL Group, a business aviation operator in Belgium and the Netherlands.
Past failures
Two German electric plane start-ups have already failed. The Munich-based company Lilium went insolvent twice before giving up for good.
A second company, Volocopter, also went insolvent and was subsequently sold to Chinese investors.
Other companies are also working on electric aircraft, including the Bavarian start-up ERC System, which is developing a plane with a hybrid engine for transporting patients and other purposes.

SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rox, which researches and develops the world's best revenue agent for the Global 2000, today announced a $100 million Series B financing at a $1.3 billion valuation.
The round is co-led by General Catalyst and March Capital, with existing investors Sequoia Capital and Factory doubling down on their investment, alongside new investors including Databricks Ventures and Prosperity7 Ventures.
In its first year in market, Rox has grown annual recurring revenue by more than 10x and is now deployed by leading public and private enterprises in non-tech industries including IT services, energy, commodities, medical technology, industrial manufacturing and automotive.
Rox is seeing more than 700% net revenue retention across enterprise customers, and some are seeing ~25x return on investment within 90 days.
The financing follows Rox's $50 million seed and Series A announced in November 2024. Zach Frankel, an early investor in Ramp, Cognition and Applied Compute, is also an early backer of Rox.
Built for the sellers who drive revenue
Enterprise sales follows a power law: the top 15% of reps bring in roughly 90% of revenue. However, the average rep spends 40% of their time on administrative work, according to Salesforce. Rox was built to raise the ceiling for those teams.
The Rox agent helps automate pipeline generation, deal execution, and upsells, so reps can better manage complex accounts and build relationships.
Agents doing real commercial work
Rox is a vertically integrated, enterprise-ready AI system built on each customer's individual data warehouse. The results are already changing sales economics:
For a global IT services firm, Rox delivered $330M in qualified pipeline in eight weeks. Reps also handed off pursuit prep to Rox and got 1,000 hours back for selling.
For a global medical technology company, Rox has identified $200M+ of new funding opportunities at medical facilities that the team is actively pursuing. Despite multi-year sales cycles for some opportunities, Rox has already helped the team close $24M in revenue in just five months.
For a leading global engineering and professional services firm, Rox identified over $310M in potential opportunities, spanning signal-qualified leads and estimated net-new pipeline from previously missed public-sector bids.
For a market-leading DevSecOps platform, Rox doubled outbound volume. Rox has transformed them into an agent-driven org and delivered millions of dollars of pipeline.
For a leading payroll provider, Rox opens up an entirely new source of growth: autonomously finding and engaging 4M prospects the sales team couldn't economically reach, and turning them into meetings at just 20% of the cost of traditional outreach.
For a global industrial software company, Rox doubled sales team capacity and delivered 50+ meetings in just six weeks.
For a large German engineering and technology company, Rox delivered 24.3x ROI in 90 days by automating sales work the business had never been able to do before, from always-on pipeline tracking to personalized outreach at scale.
Revenue is the next frontier for AI agents and one of the hardest. Unlike code, where an agent can test its work immediately, sales outcomes take weeks or months to materialize. Rox is solving that with custom models and original research, including launching a revenue-agent benchmark to measure performance on real-world revenue tasks. Rox recently cut outbound prospecting pricing by 50%, driven by research-led improvements.

Our own go-to-market runs entirely on Rox, with no other tools, and our customers are already generating hundreds of millions of dollars of pipeline at a fraction of the traditional cost. This round lets us go further in our ultimate goal of growing the world's revenue."
Rox will use the capital to advance its AI research, custom models and evaluation infrastructure, and expand its work with large enterprises across healthcare, industrial, financial services, energy and technology. We backed Ishan and his team early because of their deep expertise in enterprise sales and their proven ability to drive meaningful pipeline impact. Rox will become synonymous with revenue, and we are proud to be investors in their vision."

The system draws on the firm’s Science of Scaling framework, developed by Co-Founder and Managing Partner Mark Roberge. That framework helps companies assess when they are ready to scale and how quickly to grow.

By

Africa , Business , Funding , Investments , Startups
Enza Capital has secured a first close of $21 million for its third fund, Enza Capital III LP, which it will dedicate entirely to artificial-intelligence startups across Africa.
The pan-African venture firm, which has offices in Nairobi, Johannesburg and Cairo, is targeting $60 million for the fund with a hard cap of $80 million, and expects a final close in about a year, the firm said in an emailed statement .
The fund’s entire thesis rests on a gap. African AI, by the report’s account, attracts relatively little venture capital despite growing interest in its potential. Investors deployed about $46.8 million into African AI startups through 2026, the report says, concentrated mostly in fintech and risk-intelligence companies and modest next to AI investment in other regions.
A Briter Bridges report cited in the report found that 30% of surveyed African AI companies are entirely bootstrapped, with funding clustered among more established players; some founders say investors’ preference for proven traction makes it harder for early-stage AI companies to raise money at all.
Enza Capital is betting that the gap in African AI funding is a market failure to be exploited, not a verdict on the sector’s potential.
Enza Capital’s existing investments span SeamlessHR, Money254, Sendy, Gigmile and Peach Payments, giving a sense of the firm’s range before this fund narrows its focus specifically to AI.
That earlier spread, across HR tech, personal finance, logistics and payments, suggests Enza Capital III LP will be looking for AI applied across similarly varied sectors rather than betting narrowly on one vertical.
What to watch
The first thing to consider is the pace over the next 12 months. To move from a target of $21 million to a goal of $60 million, and even aiming for a hard cap of $80 million, it will be essential to convince limited partners that the funding gap in African AI is investable rather than simply an indicator that the market has already assessed the associated risks.
The second point to consider is whether the fund’s eventual portfolio will focus primarily on fintech and risk-intelligence companies, which have already attracted most of the continent’s AI capital, or if it will genuinely explore newer categories that the report indicates are currently underfunded and lacking institutional investment.

Index Industries Raises $50 Million in Funding to Reinvent How the World Invests in Real Estate
News provided by
Index Industries
Nov 10, 2026, 12:00 ET

Index Industries is co-founded by Josh Rosenthal, formerly the President of Polychain Capital, joining as CEO, and Brian Hardecker, CEO of Longmark and formerly of Blackstone, joining as Chairman.
The round is backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners, Galaxy Ventures, Polychain Capital, Wintermute Ventures and more.
Index Industries will launch the USHP Index, a proprietary benchmark for U.S. home prices, made investable through USHP, a liquid index product, issued by USHP Limited.
NEW YORK , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Index Industries emerges from stealth with a $50 million seed round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from Polychain Capital, Galaxy Ventures, Wintermute Ventures, and other institutional investors. The company is building the technology and infrastructure to transform U.S. housing into a broadly investable asset class. Its platform combines a daily-reporting index with tokenization technology and real estate and capital markets services to power third-party housing-linked investment products. USHP , based on Index Industries' U.S. Home Price Index and issued by USHP Limited (BVI), will be the first investment product built on the platform.
U.S. housing is a $55 trillion market, making it one of the largest asset classes in the U.S. Yet despite its scale, broad-based investment exposure to U.S. home prices has remained difficult to access through traditional financial products. Index Industries was founded to close that gap.
Index Industries' first offering will be the U.S. Home Price Index (USHP Index), a proprietary benchmark for U.S. home prices. Calculated daily, it integrates data from the major housing indices into a single national measure, providing a continuous and comprehensive read on home prices. The index is intended to support housing-market research, reporting, and portfolio monitoring and housing-related financial products.
Index Industries is co-founded by Josh Rosenthal, who joins as CEO following his role as President and General Partner of Polychain Capital, and Brian Hardecker, a former Principal at Blackstone and the Founder and CEO of Longmark, a leading residential real estate platform formed in 2021 that has $2 billion in assets under management. Index Industries combines two worlds of expertise to bring breakthrough tokenization technology to new real estate assets.
"Indexing is one of the most important and least celebrated innovations in modern finance. It reduces the expertise and cost barriers to investing in an entire market, which is what U.S. housing needs," said Josh Rosenthal, co-founder & CEO of Index Industries. "I've spent my career looking for industry-shaping financial technology, and Index Industries is exactly that. It has the potential to change how the world sees housing: not just as a roof over your head or something that is out of reach, but as an investable asset class."
"U.S. housing is a massive market. It accounts for roughly a quarter of the aggregate value of the U.S. economy, yet it draws far less attention because there haven't been accessible ways to take a position in it," said Brian Hardecker, co-founder and chairman of Index Industries and CEO of Longmark Group. "Housing is uniquely inflation-protected, uncorrelated to other asset classes, and has arguably been one of the most stable paths to wealth accumulation. It hasn't seen the benefits of financial innovation that other sectors have. That's beginning to change with USHP, and we're proud to play a role."
"Real estate is one of tokenization 's biggest opportunities, but bringing a $55 trillion asset class onchain requires traditional institutional infrastructure no crypto -native team has ever had. That's the gap Index Industries closes. It's rare to see two worlds of expertise converge at this caliber: traditional institutional rigor paired with scalable, secure, compliant technology that will unlock access and liquidity for the world's largest asset class. Index Industries' partnership with Longmark made leading this investment an easy decision for Lightspeed," said Justin Overdorff, Partner at Lightspeed Venture Partners.
Tokenization is a defining innovation in financial markets today, and the world's largest institutions are racing to adopt it. Index Industries applies tokenization to one of the most sought-after asset classes and is designed to create entirely new financial products that unlock access, income, and liquidity at institutional scale.
The USHP Index is expected to launch imminently. USHP Limited plans to release USHP in 2026 on Ethereum and expand to Solana in 2027. For more information, visit indexindustries.com .

Courier Health: Three Executives Appointed To Support Growth
Courier Health has appointed three executives to oversee its commercial, people, and customer success organizations following its $50 million Series B funding round.
Eben Scanlon joined the patient experience technology company as chief commercial officer. Mike Lamm was named chief people officer, while Phil Mishkin became senior vice president of customer success.
Scanlon will lead Courier Health’s sales and marketing teams. He previously helped clinical trial technology company Reify Health grow from an early-stage business to hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. His prior experience also includes positions at Medidata, VMware, and McKinsey & Company.
Lamm will oversee recruiting, talent development, and employee retention. He helped Squarespace prepare for and complete its public listing, supported monday.com’s expansion across the Americas, and most recently served as chief people officer at behavioral healthcare technology company RethinkFirst.
Mishkin will lead Courier Health’s post-sale organization, encompassing customer success, implementation, customer engineering, and value engineering. During eight years at Komodo Health, he built its customer success operation as the company’s customer base expanded by more than 100 times.
The appointments follow a year of increased adoption for Courier Health’s AI-native patient experience platform. The company recently introduced AI Intake and previewed AI Appeal, agents designed to automate work associated with patient enrollment and prior authorization denial appeals.
Courier Health develops software for biopharmaceutical companies managing patient access, treatment initiation, and adherence. Customers using its platform have reported double-digit improvements in patient starts, time to treatment, and continued therapy use.
The company expects its expanded leadership team to support demand from life sciences organizations seeking to modernize patient services.
