Optics11: €50 Million Funding To Expand Underwater Defense And Energy Grid Sensing Technology
Optics11, an Amsterdam-based deep technology company developing fiber-optic sensing systems for maritime security and energy infrastructure, has secured €50 million in follow-on equity financing. The investment brings the company’s total capital raised over the past 15 months to more than €100 million and will support manufacturing expansion, international growth, and increased deployment of its sensing technologies.
The latest financing was backed by existing institutional investors FORWARD.one, Value Creation Capital, SET Ventures, and JOIN Capital, with all four participating in the new round.
The investment comes as governments, defense organizations, and infrastructure operators seek additional capabilities to protect underwater assets and strengthen electricity networks.
Optics11 develops fiber-optic sensing systems designed to detect underwater activity, identify potential security threats, and monitor conditions within critical energy infrastructure.
The company’s technology originated from research at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, where its underlying photonics and acoustics capabilities were developed before Optics11 was founded in 2011.
Its sensing approach uses light to detect small acoustic signals rather than relying on powered electronics at the measurement location.
This design enables highly sensitive monitoring while remaining passive and resistant to electromagnetic interference.
The technology has applications across maritime surveillance, subsea infrastructure protection, and electrical grid monitoring.
Expanding Maritime Defense Capabilities
Optics11 is developing products intended to strengthen underwater surveillance and anti-submarine warfare capabilities.
Its OptiBarrier system provides persistent seabed sensing designed to detect and classify underwater targets at distances of up to 100 kilometers from the shoreline.
The system is intended to provide ongoing monitoring of sensitive maritime areas and infrastructure.
The company’s OptiArray platform extends its fiber-optic sensing capabilities into a mobile towed array that can be deployed from vessels.
OptiArray supports underwater intelligence gathering, maritime surveillance, and anti-submarine warfare operations.
Earlier in 2026, the Dutch Ministry of Defence selected Optics11’s containerized OptiArray technology for the ASWINABO program, also known as Anti-Submarine Warfare In A Box.
The program aims to provide advanced underwater sensing capabilities through a wider range of maritime platforms.
These include crewed and uncrewed surface vessels, as well as certain civilian ships.
The initiative is intended to improve the Royal Netherlands Navy’s readiness and operational flexibility.
Optics11 considers the selection an important validation of its technology and a potential foundation for additional defense deployments.
The company sees increased interest in maritime sensing systems as European governments reassess their ability to monitor underwater activity and protect critical infrastructure.
Strengthening Electricity Grid Monitoring
Optics11 also applies its sensing technology to electrical infrastructure through its OptiFinder platform.
OptiFinder is designed to detect and locate partial discharge activity within high-voltage electrical equipment.
Partial discharge can be an early indication of insulation degradation and developing faults inside assets such as transformers.
Identifying these conditions before equipment failure can help infrastructure operators plan maintenance and reduce operational disruptions.
OptiFinder uses fiber-optic acoustic sensing to provide information about potential problems within high-voltage assets.
The technology is already deployed in operational environments internationally.
Electricity networks are facing increased pressure from electrification, higher power demand, and the need to improve infrastructure reliability.
Optics11 believes these developments will create additional opportunities for advanced monitoring systems capable of identifying equipment problems at an early stage.
Scaling Manufacturing And International Operations
The company plans to use its new capital to increase manufacturing capacity and expand international operations.
The investment will also support delivery of existing orders and development of relationships with government agencies, industrial companies, and infrastructure operators.
Optics11 reported growing international demand across both maritime security and energy grid applications.
Its expanding order book and commercial pipeline reflect interest in sensing technologies that provide earlier detection and more detailed information than certain conventional approaches.
The company intends to increase its ability to manufacture and deploy systems while continuing product development.
With more than €100 million invested over 15 months, Optics11 is positioning itself to expand its role in protecting maritime and electrical infrastructure.
The financing supports its transition toward broader commercial deployment as demand increases across defense and energy markets.

Mosaic Raises $47M Seed to Develop Spatial Intelligence for Surgery
Published

By
Nova Jain, AI Entrepreneurship & Founders AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Mosaic Intelligence Labs announced on November 10, 2026 that it had emerged from stealth with $47 million in seed funding to develop sensing-enabled spatial intelligence and robotic systems for surgery, initially focusing on procedures performed through the vascular system.
The San Francisco company named 8VC, Fundomo, Lingotto Innovation and Obvious Ventures among its backers. Chief executive Ileana Pirozzi and chief technology officer Alison “Ali” Kight Mackanic founded Mosaic after meeting during their doctoral studies at Stanford. Their work alongside clinicians exposed how difficult, less-invasive procedures often remain tied to knowledge held by individual operators.
“We kept returning to one question: what would it take to scale the knowledge of the very best surgeons?” Pirozzi said. “We believe that starts with making our machines aware, and turning surgical repetition into experience we can learn from.”
Starting With Endovascular Procedures
Mosaic’s initial target is endovascular care. In these procedures, physicians thread flexible wires and catheters through blood vessels to reach treatment sites. Mosaic describes blood vessels as routes to virtually every organ, yet operators have no direct line of sight inside them. They use live X-ray imaging, preoperative scans and the feel of the instruments to work out where they are and what lies ahead.
The company identifies radiation exposure and outcomes that vary with operator experience as limitations of that workflow. Interpreting the available signals can take years of practice, and much of the resulting knowledge is difficult to record or hand down. The result is a mismatch: surgical access has become less invasive, while navigation still depends heavily on the perception and judgment of the person holding the instrument.
For context, Mosaic’s website compares open surgery’s 20–30 cm incision and keyhole surgery’s 1–2 cm ports with endovascular surgery’s 2 mm needle puncture, and lists stopping strokes, clearing blocked coronary arteries, repairing aneurysms and restoring blood flow to limbs among current applications. That range helps explain why Mosaic is treating vascular navigation as a reusable capability across multiple procedures.
Giving Surgical Instruments a Learning Loop
The technical design begins by instrumenting the point where surgical tools meet anatomy. Mosaic intends to combine those sensor readings with computation that reconstructs the vascular environment from within, maintaining a three-dimensional picture of anatomy and instrument position as it changes. A robotic interface would support precise instrument control.
The learning architecture would record the environment, instrument movement and physician actions as synchronized streams. Physical models would then help the system relate what it senses to what happens when it moves. The release connects this approach to the robotics concept of a world model: a representation of an environment that helps a machine predict how its actions will change that environment.
All of these capabilities remain development goals; the announcement supplies no patient-outcome findings or clinical-performance results. The nearer objective is to assist physicians’ perception and control, while the recorded procedures are intended to become a source of cumulative learning for machines over time.
Recruiting and Longer-Term Treatment Goals
Mosaic is recruiting engineers, physicians and creatives in San Francisco. Open roles cover hardware engineering, sensing, perception, machine learning and clinical engineering, matching a technical effort that spans physical instruments, software, robotics and clinical practice.
Mosaic’s longer-term goal is to widen the treatments delivered through these vascular routes. The company says catheters can deliver drugs, energy, biologics and other therapies directly to a target site, and that more reliable navigation could expand both the range of treatments delivered through blood vessels and the settings in which clinicians can offer them.
Mosaic’s near-term product challenge and longer-term data ambition are linked: dependable navigation must work in individual procedures before those procedures can provide a useful foundation for cumulative machine learning.

Star Holdings: Q3 Revenue Reaches $39.9 Million As Net Loss Widens To $45.1 Million
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 7:50 AM
Star Holdings: Q3 Revenue Reaches $39.9 Million As Net Loss Widens To $45.1 Million
Star Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $39.9 million, up from $28.1 million a year earlier, as land development activity increased. The real estate-focused company nevertheless recorded a net loss of $45.1 million, compared with net income of $274,000 in the third quarter of 2025.
Operating lease income was $1.7 million, compared with $1.8 million a year earlier. Interest income and other operating sources contributed to the quarter, while land development revenue increased to $21 million from $1.7 million. The company recognized revenue from the sale of a land parcel during the period, with related development cost of sales reducing the transaction’s contribution.
The loss allocable to common shareholders was $45.1 million, or $3.74 per share, compared with income allocable to common shareholders of $1.8 million, or $0.14 per share, in the prior-year quarter. Results reflected the timing of property transactions, carrying costs, interest expense, and changes in the value or performance of Star’s remaining assets and investments.
For the first nine months of 2026, total revenue was $80.2 million, compared with $84.8 million a year earlier. The nine-month net loss narrowed to $18.1 million from $47.5 million, while the loss allocable to common shareholders improved to $13.9 million from $45.1 million.
Star Holdings was created to hold and realize value from a portfolio of legacy real estate assets and other investments. Its results can vary significantly between periods because land sales, loan repayments, hotel activity, and asset dispositions do not occur on a uniform schedule. Third-quarter revenue growth therefore showed progress in monetizing property, but the substantial reported loss demonstrated the continuing costs and valuation effects associated with managing the portfolio. Future performance will depend heavily on the timing and economics of additional asset sales, development activity, and resolution of remaining obligations.

Dreeze Emerges From Stealth With $33M to Rebuild Cloud Apps After Cyberattacks
Created by Zerto and Kashya veterans, the startup has launched a platform designed to recover whole cloud applications.
By

Cloud application recovery startup Dreeze announced on Tuesday that it raised $33 million in a seed funding round as it emerged from stealth mode with a platform built to bring back whole cloud applications instead of only the data behind them.
The round was led by Norwest and Bessemer Venture Partners, with Claltech also investing.
Dreeze , whose staff is split between Israel and the United States, said the money will go toward product development, bigger sales and marketing teams, and getting its platform into more enterprises.
The company was formed in 2025 by Avi Raichel and brothers Ziv and Oded Kedem. The three previously worked together at Zerto, which HPE acquired , and Kashya.
Dreeze’s argument is that getting data back after an incident is not the same as getting an application running again. A cyberattack or a mistake by an AI agent can leave an organization with its data intact but without the configurations, secrets, infrastructure and connections the application needs.
Its platform, named Application Revival, scans the customer’s cloud environment on an ongoing basis, works out which resources and dependencies belong to which application, and generates a recovery plan from the live environment. Backups of data and configurations are stored with those recovery plans in an immutable, isolated vault under the customer’s control.
Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.
In a recovery scenario, Application Revival automatically reconstructs the application as a whole. Customers can also run recovery tests in an isolated account, with no impact on production.
“Companies have spent years getting better at backing up data, but getting the data back doesn’t mean the business is back,” said Ziv Kedem, the company’s CEO. “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down.”
“We started Dreeze because recovery needs to go further. Our goal is to make Application Revival the new standard, so companies know they have a proven path to bring their applications back when something goes wrong,” he added.
The AWS version of the platform is generally available. Support for Microsoft Azure is in early access, with general availability expected in early 2027.

Backed by Kleiner Perkins and Costanoa, Nidus brings intelligent, autonomous systems that dramatically increase factory output, beginning with the wire harnesses inside every aircraft, missile, and vehicle
NEW YORK , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nidus, the robotics company deploying embodied intelligence inside America's defense factories, announced $30 million in funding today, backed by Kleiner Perkins and Costanoa, with participation from Ludlow Ventures, SF1, Absolute Partners, Tau, and angel investors, including Chris Power, founder of Hadrian; Adrian Aoun, co-founder of Dulo, Foundational Industries and Seneca; and Nikhil Goel, Chief Commercial Officer at Archer.
America's defense industrial base has a capacity crisis. The country that once produced more than half the world's goods now relies heavily on overseas supply chains to manufacture parts for its own weapons systems. This constitutes a national security risk, and factories urgently need to increase output to meet demand.
Nidus builds embodied intelligence that lets traditional industrial robots perform precision assembly tasks. The company develops and deploys foundation robotics models across America's critical defense factories, using sovereign AI training practices. This lets each customer retain its collective knowledge, which is crucial in secure environments.
"I grew up in rural South Carolina and watched offshoring create the current industrial base crisis," said Justin Sealy, co-founder and CEO of Nidus. "At this point, we can't out-labor or out-scale our competition. We need to leapfrog the rest of the world by deploying physical AI that scales America's existing industrial capacity. This is why we started Nidus."
Nidus is deploying across the defense industrial base and quickly eclipsed seven figures in revenue in its first four months. The company is currently delivering customized models to automate wire processing on its proprietary platform, which was built from the ground up to meet Department of War security requirements.
"In physical AI, the value will accrue to players that prioritize deployment and customer value. And Nidus is the rare team that has actually deployed AI into the most locked-down environments in the country" said Aatish Nayak, partner at Kleiner Perkins. "The demand they're seeing is a testament to the value of their mission and product. We're thrilled to back Justin, Charu, Harrison, and Cane as they bring AI to the factories America's security depends on."
"The U.S. cannot rebuild industrial capacity through new construction alone. Nidus is taking a different approach, using AI and robotics to increase production inside existing factories," said Greg Sands, Founder and Managing Partner at Costanoa. "We backed Justin and the team at pre-seed because of their firsthand experience with the challenges of American manufacturing and their technical ability to address them. We believe Nidus has the potential to make a meaningful difference in how critical products are manufactured in the U.S."
Nidus will use this funding to grow its engineering team, expand from wire-harness automation into additional factory workflows, and scale production deployments with U.S. defense manufacturers.
"We only build for American institutions that are vital for securing democracy," added Sealy. "We believe in a future where American industry is self-sustaining and no longer dependent on foreign production. We're building the infrastructure to make that future a reality."
About Nidus
Nidus is the leading developer of industrial AI, purpose-built to augment America's manufacturing base. We are on a mission to equip the factories that enable American industry with embodied intelligence that radically scales operations. Founded by a team with decades of experience across machine learning, robotics, hardware, and defense tech, Nidus brings foundation models out of the lab and onto the factory floor. Finite State has raised $27 million in Series C funding to expand its AI-driven product security platform and international operations. The round was led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund , with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking , Energy Impact Partners , Energize Capital , and National Grid Partners .
The Columbus, Ohio-based company focuses on a problem that becomes more consequential as vulnerability discovery accelerates: manufacturers need to know what software actually runs inside the devices they sell. A flaw in a shared component can affect vehicles, medical equipment, industrial systems, or consumer electronics, but determining which finished products contain that component can be difficult.
Finite State plans to use the capital to deepen its presence in international markets and develop more autonomous platform capabilities. Its technology combines analysis of software artifacts with vulnerability intelligence and compliance workflows, aiming to turn an inventory of shipped code into decisions about what needs attention.
Inspecting the Software That Actually Ships
Connected products are assembled from many sources: an operating system, open-source libraries, supplier SDKs, board-support packages, and proprietary applications. Manufacturers may control their own source code while having limited visibility into compiled components supplied by other vendors.
A build manifest describes what a development process expects to include. Firmware analysis examines the artifact produced by that process. The difference matters when packaging adds a component, a supplier modifies a library, or a dependency is compiled directly into an executable.
Finite State’s binary-analysis documentation describes unpacking firmware images, containers, archives, and executables, then identifying components through binary software composition analysis. It also applies static application security testing to compiled code, examining weaknesses beyond a simple list of package names.
The resulting inventory can include modified and statically linked components, with findings enriched by vulnerability, exploit, and license information. The analysis also looks for hard-coded credentials, exposed keys, and cryptographic issues. Supported inputs include firmware, shared libraries, mobile application binaries, and third-party software, as well as source code when available.
This is the foundation of the company’s pitch: security decisions should follow the contents of the finished product, rather than depend entirely on the documentation that accompanies it.
Turning a Component Inventory Into a Remediation Decision
Finding a vulnerable component is only the beginning. A product team still needs to determine whether the affected code can be reached, whether an exploit is relevant to the device’s configuration, and which releases or product variants need a fix.
Finite State’s platform overview describes prioritization based on reachability, exploit intelligence, and product context. The aim is to reduce the time engineers spend investigating findings that do not represent the same level of practical exposure.
A software bill of materials, or SBOM, records the components in a product. Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange, or VEX, adds information about whether a particular vulnerability affects that product. Together, those records help distinguish an inventory question—whether a component is present—from an assessment of the risk it creates.
Finite State says its platform can identify known and previously unknown vulnerabilities. That combines different kinds of analysis: matching components against disclosed issues and examining compiled code for weaknesses. The usefulness of the result depends on the evidence behind a finding and its relevance to the device, not simply the number of alerts produced.
AI Automation Still Needs Evidence About Analysis Quality
One practical example of the company’s AI work is its AI Unpacking Evaluation Agent , introduced earlier in 2026. The agent evaluates how completely an uploaded artifact was extracted and explains gaps that may limit the subsequent analysis.
That step is important because a scan cannot assess code it never successfully extracted. Encrypted containers, nested archives, or unusual firmware packaging can leave part of an artifact outside the scanner’s view.
Finite State says the agent supplies a quality rating, identifies likely causes of incomplete extraction, and recommends actions such as decrypting content, unpacking it locally, or repackaging an archive before another upload. The automation helps teams understand what the analysis covered, rather than treating every completed scan as equally comprehensive.
The broader platform connects that analysis to reviewable workflows. Its published architecture describes bringing firmware, binaries, source code, supplier SBOMs, and documentation into a common process for generating security findings, verification evidence, and reports.

The financing announcement places regulatory pressure alongside faster vulnerability discovery as a driver of demand. Manufacturers increasingly need evidence showing how they identified software risks, assessed their impact, and addressed them across the product lifecycle.

Productivity gurus online these days say AI agents should book your travel, manage calendars, and send emails. Lumbra thinks they can do a whole lot more, and so far, a rapidly growing list of customers in the intelligence community and the Pentagon agree. Investors do too.
This morning, the DC-based AI startup announced a $25M Series A to keep scaling its AI agent operating system and agent harness across the defense and national security space and expand into “regulated commercial sectors,” the company told Tectonic exclusively.
Point 72 Ventures and Ansa Capital co-led the round, with participation from the company’s OG backer, Costanoa Ventures.
Secret agent: Founded by ex-Army Ranger and CIA counterterrorism officer Aaron Brown (CEO) and fellow Ranger—and MIT-trained computer scientist—Michael Hiebert (CTO), Lumbra’s pitch is that AI agents have the potential to be incredibly capable tools for analysts and decision-makers in national security, but they need the right operating framework, or harness, to make their analysis work auditable, verifiable, and trustworthy.
Lumbra’s platform, called LumbraOS, does that with three core offerings:
Nebula is the agent orchestrator that records actions, traces claims to sources, and enforces data protection. The human running the agents fact-checks those findings and analysis workflows before they’re relayed to a system of record.
StarChart is a customer organization’s knowledge graph where agents automatically compound knowledge as they work, with “insights and conclusions recorded alongside sources and sensitivity labels,” according to Lumbra.
Astrolabe is the agent evaluator that tests them before deployment and tracks scores in production using the customer’s benchmarks.
Put simply, “We’re building a coordination layer for intelligence advantage and decision intelligence—it’s the harness, it’s the control panel, the control layer, it’s the consumption layer,” Brown told Tectonic . “We’re putting the controls in place, the data lineage, the explainability, the coordination layer, the benchmark, and the evaluations, plus the harness.”
The platform is “model-neutral” (as opposed to model-agnostic), meaning it can run a range of frontier and open-source models depending on the performance level required for the task agents are running.
“To do some of these tasks, there’s a level of ability that the model has to be above,” Brown said. “It just needs to be a model that is at that level of performance, so we’re model neutral with strong model opinions.”
Rolling out: So far, that’s proven to be a hit with intelligence community customers—where Lumbra signed its first contracts—and increasingly with a self-proclaimed “AI-first” Defense Department. Lumbra is already under contract, with its agents in production on top-secret networks across the Pentagon and IC.
Lumbra was one of two companies—the other being a small company you might’ve heard of called Palantir— tapped by the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) for the “Agent Network” Pace-Setting Project under the Department’s AI Acceleration Strategy.
Under that contract, Lumbra is responsible for implementing “AI orchestration technology operational on US Government systems” to “compress the time it takes to turn intelligence into informed options for commanders around the world.”
The trust element is a big reason for Lumbra’s hot start with defense customers and on classified networks.
“There are a lot of different ways you can slice up these potential agentic systems. For us, especially when it’s leading to a consequential decision, everything needs the ability to be explained,” Brown said. “You need to be able to allow a human, who’s cognitively limited compared to these machines, to be able to consume that quickly and say, ‘All right, now I trust this output because I read it with my own eyes.’”
That said, Brown doesn’t think agents are ready to take over all elements of the intelligence analysis workflow—especially targeting decisions.
“I say over and over again, these systems are nowhere near ready enough to do any type of automated targeting work—I wouldn’t trust it; nobody should trust it,” he said. “What they can do, which is spectacular, is help humans know much more about a target than they would ever be able to know on their own.”
Growing up and out: With a fresh $25M in the bank, Lumbra is looking to take that validation earned in the most high-consequence environments into the commercial world, especially in highly regulated sectors. According to Brown, the company is already “working with some private companies in a B2B relationship—some very big ones.”
For a startup that itself is “agent-pilled,” as Brown put it, he’s betting that Lumbra will be “one of the first examples of a 100-200 person company that swings like a 2,000-3,000 person company,” he said. “I don’t think anyone who’s touching our product right now would say anything other than we’re at the front edge of this compared to anyone else in the game.”

AbbVie Ventures and Lumination Capital joining existing lead investors Samsara BioCapital and Lightstone Ventures
Financing supports TNFα development candidate nomination and initiation of IND-enabling studies, alongside advancement of oral TL1A inhibitors into lead optimization
Proprietary QUAISAR platform, combined with approach to Physical AI, continues to drive rapid design of optimized oral drug candidates
WATERTOWN, Mass., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- PsiThera, a biotechnology company harnessing biologically relevant protein states and physical artificial intelligence to create oral drugs for immune and inflammatory diseases, today announced the closing of a $25 million financing. New investors AbbVie Ventures and Lumination Capital participated, along with existing lead investors Samsara BioCapital and Lightstone Ventures, and other existing investors. In connection with the financing, Claire Leurent, Ph.D., MBA, Managing Director at AbbVie Ventures, has joined PsiThera’s Board of Directors.
Proceeds from the financing are expected to fund operations, supporting development candidate nomination and the initiation of IND-enabling studies for the company’s lead oral small molecule TNFα inhibitor, as well as advancement of its oral TL1A program into lead optimization.
The company’s proprietary QUAISAR platform combines physics-based molecular simulation, machine learning, and experimental biophysics into a single closed-loop discovery engine to design novel small molecule therapeutics more efficiently. QUAISAR models protein motion to identify and target transient binding pockets that conventional structure-based design cannot see, enabling the design of small molecules for targets that have been difficult to address with oral therapies. Using this platform, PsiThera advanced the company’s lead TNFα program from hit identification to lead optimization in just four months.
“Our goal is to bring the efficacy of leading biologics into novel oral medicines to improve on their therapeutic profiles. This financing accelerates our progress toward that vision as we advance our oral TNFα program toward development candidate nomination and clinical initiation and expand our pipeline of differentiated immunology therapeutics, starting with TL1A,” said Eric D. Shaff, President and Chief Executive Officer of PsiThera. “We are grateful for the continued support of our existing investors and welcome AbbVie Ventures and Lumination Capital.”
Injectable anti-TNFα biologic therapies are approved across a broad range of immune-mediated diseases. However, an oral therapeutic could have broad application, both as monotherapy and as a combination partner, and provide an additional treatment option to the many patients who have not yet started biologic therapy.
PsiThera’s oral TNFα inhibitors are designed to achieve a differentiated profile to improve the therapeutic index relative to injectables or other oral TNFα inhibitors in development, supporting best-in-class potential.
“PsiThera has brought together seasoned biopharma leadership, experienced drug hunters, and immunology and computational scientists around a platform that can find and exploit protein states that conventional approaches cannot effectively drug,” said Christina Isacson, Ph.D., Chair of PsiThera’s Board of Directors and Partner at Lightstone Ventures. “Our progress with TNFα and TL1A is illustrative of the power of the platform. With this financing, the Company is well-positioned to advance its lead programs and extend its platform across a broader immunology pipeline.”
About PsiThera
PsiThera is a biotechnology company harnessing biologically relevant protein states and physical artificial intelligence to create oral drugs for immune and inflammatory diseases, therapeutic areas historically reliant on injectables. By integrating biophysics, computational modeling, and mechanistic biology through its QUAISAR platform, PsiThera’s expert drug hunters discover new therapeutic opportunities and optimized drugs. The company’s initial programs target clinically validated cytokine pathways, including TNFα, TL1A, and IL-6. PsiThera is headquartered in Watertown, Massachusetts. Американский стартап привлёк $20 млн на космические аппараты, которые сами собираются на орбите
Новости
Rendezvous Robotics
28 октября стартап Rendezvous Robotics из Голдена в штате Колорадо объявил о посевном раунде на $20 млн. Его возглавили венчурные компании MaC Venture Capital и Toyota Ventures, а средства пойдут на разработку нового поколения аппаратов, лётные демонстрации и расширение команды.
Помимо лидеров, в раунде участвовали фонд University of Michigan Endowment, Astera, Industrious Ventures, Humbition и NextView Ventures. Компанию и дальше поддержали существующие инвесторы Aurelia Foundry, ATX Venture Partners и Mana Ventures.
- Реклама -
Стартап ищет выход из ограничений, которые накладывает запуск. Большинство аппаратов проектируют так, чтобы они поместились в головной обтекатель — защитную оболочку на вершине ракеты, под которой летит груз. Из-за этого ещё до запуска приходится идти на компромиссы в выработке энергии, вычислительных мощностях, размере антенн и теплоотводе, хотя потребность во всём этом растёт.
Гендиректор Джо Лэндон пояснил Payload, что отрасль не хочет аппаратов меньшего размера и меньшей мощности. «Никто не говорит о том, чтобы делать спутники меньше и менее функциональными, — сказал он. — Все хотят больше мощности, больше теплоотвода, более крупные антенны, более чувствительную связь. Но этого не достичь, пока мы не научимся строить прямо в космосе».
Подписывайтесь на Mediasat в Telegram : здесь самые интересные новости из мира технологий
Rendezvous Robotics предлагает другой подход — аппарат из компактных независимых модулей-плиток. Их запускают по отдельности, а на орбите они самостоятельно маневрируют, выравниваются и соединяются в одну конструкцию, которую после запуска можно перестроить под новые задачи. Этот подход вырос из почти десятилетних исследований соосновательницы компании Ариэль Экблау в Массачусетском технологическом институте (MIT) в рамках программы TESSERAE. Ранние поколения TESSERAE уже проверяли на суборбитальной ракете New Shepard компании Blue Origin и во время двух миссий на Международной космической станции (МКС).
Сейчас Rendezvous Robotics разрабатывает новое поколение более крупных независимых модулей, а их движение, выравнивание и сборку проверяет на Земле. Эти испытания продолжат серией параболических полётов в ноябре 2026 года, во время которых самолёт ненадолго создаёт невесомость. В этих полётах испытают электромагнитный привод и движение модулей. Отдельно от них, в декабре на МКС, проведут заключительную демонстрацию TESSERAE пятого поколения — 32 плитки должны автономно собраться в трёхмерную конструкцию.
Демонстрационную миссию на низкой околоземной орбите запланировали не ранее апреля 2028 года. В ней семь независимых модулей должны автономно соединиться в один аппарат, разделиться и снова собраться в иной конфигурации без помощи внешних роботизированных манипуляторов. Компания называет её первой в своём роде и уже зарезервировала место в совместном запуске (rideshare), где модули выведут на орбиту вместе с другими грузами.
Модульность даёт и практическую выгоду. Оператор может менять конфигурацию аппарата, добавлять новые модули или заменять неисправные прямо на орбите, а не строить и запускать новый аппарат. По словам Лэндона, нынешнее обслуживание спутников сводится к продлению срока службы, тогда как система Rendezvous при повреждении может сама изменить свою структуру на лучшую из доступных. Лэндон допускает и создание на орбите склада модулей, который будет выдавать запасные части по требованию.

COLUMBIA, Md. , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- iCareManager, a leading EHR and care management platform purpose-built for providers supporting people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD), today announced a strategic growth investment from Five Elms Capital. The partnership will accelerate product innovation, expand AI capabilities, grow the leadership team, and extend iCareManager's reach to more provider organizations across the U.S.

IDD providers operate in one of healthcare's most complex environments, navigating state-specific Medicaid waivers, service authorizations, billing, EVV, medication management, and compliance amid workforce shortages and financial pressure. Since 2011, iCareManager has simplified these challenges with technology built specifically for the IDD community.
iCareManager is a unified platform that connects clinical care, service delivery, compliance, workforce management, and billing for human services providers. It brings person-centered planning, eMAR, documentation, scheduling, and Medicaid billing into one view, with built-in support for state-specific rules and EVV. "Over the years, we've built iCareManager with a clear purpose: to make technology work better for the people who provide support and care," said Kamal Sheikh, Co-Founder and CEO of iCareManager. "We're now entering a new era where AI will fundamentally change how people work and interact with technology. The next generation of software won't just help people manage their work; it will increasingly work alongside them. Five Elms understands what we've built, the market we serve, and where we want to go. Scalestack: Alysio Acquisition And Leonis-Led Funding Expand Enterprise AI Agent Controls
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 2:10 AM
Scalestack: Alysio Acquisition And Leonis-Led Funding Expand Enterprise AI Agent Controls
Scalestack has raised new funding led by Leonis Capital and acquired AI agent workspace Alysio, expanding its platform for controlling how autonomous agents access enterprise data, execute tasks and interact with business systems. Zapier, Deel and AAF participated in the financing. Scalestack will use the capital to grow its engineering and go-to-market teams and develop additional governance and orchestration capabilities.
The New York-based company provides infrastructure connecting AI agents with systems such as customer relationship management platforms, applicant tracking software, enterprise resource planning systems and data warehouses.
Its platform supplies agents with business context, applies company rules and controls what they can read, write and spend. It also records actions, changes and associated costs.
Alysio adds a workspace where agents execute tasks, extending Scalestack’s existing context and business rules capabilities into the environment where work takes place.
Scalestack says its platform already processes more than 6 million records per quarter for dozens of enterprise customers. At Typeform, it turns more than 400,000 monthly form submissions into context for downstream workflows, with reported accuracy above 90%.
DigitalOcean uses the platform to apply territory rules before information is written back to Salesforce. Recruiting company Hueman rebuilt candidate screening around workflows that apply hiring policies and record decisions, reducing time to a decision from nine days to the same day, according to the announcement.
At Clio, Scalestack connects a data lake, external data vendors, agent-based research and Salesforce. Clio has built more than 30 autonomous workflows on the platform, with business rules governing information written back to its system of record.
The next development phase includes a gateway that applies enterprise rules to requests from different agents and models, alongside infrastructure for persistent agents operating in cloud and local environments.
KEY QUOTES:
“Soon, most of the work inside any enterprise will be done by agents and, over time, no enterprise will hand that work to a model it doesn’t control. Companies will own the context and the rules their agents run on, and every action will be checked, governed and recorded, whichever model comes next. That is the layer we are building, and our customers already run on it. With Leonis, strong corporate partners, and the Alysio acquisition, we can get there faster.”
Elio Narciso, Co-Founder And CEO Of Scalestack
“As AI agents move from answering questions to taking actions, the bottleneck is shifting from model intelligence to enterprise trust and control. Every company will need a way to give agents the right context, enforce business rules and govern their actions across systems. We believe Scalestack is building a foundational layer of this new enterprise architecture, and its traction with major customers gives us conviction that this shift is already underway.”
Jay Zhao, Managing Partner Of Leonis Capital
“Agents are only as good as the data underneath them. Scalestack’s ability to turn high-volume raw data into actionable context pairs naturally with the workflows our customers run on Zapier. We’re glad to back them.”
Wade Foster, Co-Founder And CEO Of Zapier
